item.title: Allendale - 5L11
item.description:
From CaveDB

Known as the ‘hole in the middle of the road’, Allendale is one the of the first CDAA Cave Rated sites that divers have access in the earlier steps of their cave training. The cave consists of a main straight tunnel on a 45 degrees slope reaching 26m depth at the bottom and a total 60m length (from surface to deepest part). A small surface lake can host divers comfortably with water level usually at below waist level. The Northwest corner of the lake will grant access to the cave’s main tunnel which is reasonably large until you reach 12m depth after a 25m swim. Attentive divers will notice on their right hand side that some sort of collapse happened there. The main tunnel branches East at the 12 m restriction, and one can navigate through a narrow passage until hitting a full stop after a roughly 15 metres swim. Back to the main tunnel and once cleared the 12m depth mark, divers will face a large room spanning 30m in length (to the deepest part of the cave) and 20m in width. Behind the black silt pile on the Northwest corner a fissure on the rock has been object of many divers work. She doesn’t go, yet…

item.title: Bakers Cave - 5L285
item.description:
From CaveDB

🗺️ Site Overview

The site features a vertical solution tube approximately 1 meter in diameter, descending around 16 meters to reach the water. Divers can swim to a clean rock in waist-deep water, which serves as a stable platform for donning or doffing dive gear.

The dive itself includes a spacious underwater main chamber that connects to a tunnel reaching a maximum depth of 33 meters.

item.title: Fossil Cave - 5L81
item.description:
From CaveDB

Fossil cave is named for the fossils found there so care must be taken not to disturb these. It is a doline collapse that has east and west dives. The west side is a shortish cave level dive that has many nooks and cranies to explore. The west is bigger and rated cave for the most part but there is a restriction at 13m that you must be cave rated to pass and enters the tank cave system.

item.title: Iddlebiddy Cave - 5L250
item.description:
From CaveDB

Iddlebiddy Cave is a 250m single passage-way, which runs from the entrance chamber and ends in a small, silty room containing an array of largely-formed clay deposits.

Divers must take care when venturing into this cave, as the soft walls and delicate features located in the long passage make the water susceptible to clouding. Divers are encouraged to take their time passing through the passage, to enjoy the many cave features and avoid causing finning or physical damage.

item.title: Jam Cave - 5L301
item.description:
From CaveDB

BC visited 04/23: 70 cm hole descending straight down. Need ropes to enter exit, ideally an ascender as it is a hard climb out. Opens in 5m cavern area with big mound in the center that looks like accumulation or someone trying to fill it. Area at the bottom of the pile has fresh water in it. Digging is hard and there will be a lot of material to remove for any hope of progressing.

item.title: Kilbsy's Sinkhole - 5L46
item.description:
From CaveDB

Kilsby Sinkhole is a naturally occurring karst sinkhole located on private property 10 kilometres south-west of Mount Gambier in South Australia. The sinkhole is renowned worldwide for its crystal clear water and extensive open caverns, making it a popular destination for recreational diving. The site is accessible only via prior bookings, which can be made online or by phone.

Kilsby Sinkhole is the only site of its kind in Australia that welcomes snorkellers and Open Water certified divers, through to those with Cave or Technical dive training. Snorkellers, Freedivers and Open Water divers must be guided by an approved Dive Instructor. With a depth of almost 30 metres directly from the pontoon, the site is a perfect location for freediving and training camps are regularly held onsite.

item.title: Little Blue Lake - 5L9
item.description:
From CaveDB

Little Blue is a commonly used as a local swimming hole as well as being a popular basic cave diving site. It is relatively easy to access from the road and has a decent equipment assembly table and stairs running straight down to the water. The clarity can be quite poor and it is relatively deep getting down to nearly 40m. You should take care on your air consumption and non deco time as you will run into deco quite quickly. Visibility can be quite poor especially in the top 20m and there is little to see beyond random junk that has been thrown into it over the years. The rubbish include barbed wire and other random items so take care around the bottom not to get snagged. During summer months it can be full of locals swimming and dive bombing from the top so be careful not to get landed on.

item.title: Nettlebed - 5L290
item.description:
From CaveDB

Nettlebed Cave is home to a range of interesting features for cave divers to explore. The wall-scratchings which can seen once inside “The Gallery” are probable evidence of megafauna, while entrenched seashells provide insight into the cave’s Ice Age inhabitants.

Beyond The Gallery, the cave drops deeper and breaks into additional rooms containing many large, dark silt-covered boulders, black walls and white-clay floored passages.

The cave finishes in a chamber at 28m, but with an actual penetration distance from the surface of 80m.

item.title: Picanninnie Ponds - 5L72 - CLOSED
item.description:
From CaveDB

Piccaninnie Ponds is a karst sinkhole located in the Limestone Coast region of South Australia, approximately 32 kilometres southeast of Mount Gambier. The site is recognized as a wetland of international importance and is listed under the Ramsar Convention. The ponds are renowned for their crystal-clear water, which supports aquatic vegetation up to 15 metres below the surface.

Piccaninnie Ponds is a popular destination for recreational diving, attracting both snorkelers and cave divers. The site contains three main features of interest to cave divers: The First Pond, an open depression about 10 metres deep with a silt floor and much aquatic life; The Chasm, a sinkhole over 100 metres deep; and The Cathedral, a large underwater cavern with majestic white walls of sculptured and scalloped limestone.

item.title: Tank Cave - 5L230
item.description:
From CaveDB

Tank cave in Mount Gambia, South Australia is one of Australia’s most popular and largest mapped submerged cave. It has over 7km of passage of which most contain fixed lines. It is located in farmland about 20km outside Mount Gambia and its entrance is on land owned by the Cave Divers Association of Australia. The cave is a complex system of interconnected tunnels that requires complex navigation and even after gaining the needed advance cave standard you need to follow a strict familiarization schedule consisting of 18 dives that progressively expand your experience of the system. Care must be taken with planning and cookie discipline due the complexity of dives and particular care taken not to cut corners and potentially miss an obscured branch of line. A large amount of the cave are accessible to back-mount divers but many sections required side-mount configuration to penetrate. Water temperature is relatively constant 14 Celsius year round and a dry suit with suitable thermal protected is needed. Much of the cave is quite shallow around 10-12 metres with deeper sections as you get to the Fossil Cave side getting to 20+ metres.

item.title: The Shaft - 5L158
item.description:
From CaveDB

The Shaft is a sinkhole located near Mount Gambier in South Australia. It is a popular destination for cave divers, known for its clear water and interesting internal structure.

The Shaft is the site of a tragic scuba diving incident that occurred on May 28, 1973, which claimed the lives of four recreational scuba divers. The incident led to the formation of the Cave Divers Association of Australia and the development of the South Australian Police Underwater Recovery Squad .
